I'm not a fan of the power switch being BELOW the volume rocker - the phone is relatively large, and when holding it, your thumb fairly naturally rests on the power switch, which isn't all that useful. The fingerprint reader works well, and the Motorola app allows programming of the reader to do a 'back' and 'home' command, freeing up some screen space, which is cool. I turned off the long-press on the fingerprint reader to turn off the device, because it was far to easy to turn the phone off - the 'long press' must be like a second - I found myself accidentally turning the phone off far too often.

Anyhoo, the biggest gripe I have by far with the phone isn't actually the phones fault - it's Android. Out of the box with Android 7, there's no way to tell if you have unread e-mails - the apps don't have 'badges'. Coming from iOS, this is hugely annoying. I know in some cases this can be restored with a change of launder and a bunch of configuration, but it's a crappy annoyance to deal with. Supposedly this might be fixed in the new version of Android.

So, overall - it's a nice phone. Not the fastest in the world, but it doesn't well enough for normal use. Good battery life, good build quality, nice screen, and all of the pro's and con's of Android.

Once last comment - I don't find the Amazon stuff too intrusive. By default there is a widget set up to show Amazon sales, but it is easily removed like any other widget. Once you do that, the only real Amazon thing that is forced on you is an add on the unlock screen - not a biggie.

review_title: Best Android Phone But Not Perfect Of Course
review_text:
You can argue about numbers on paper comparing with other flagship phones from other less mainstream brands (or iPhone.) But after two weeks of use, coming from a Note 20 Ultra, I can say this is most likely the best mainstream brand Android Smartphone out there. Is it worth upgrading from the S22 Ultra? Only if you are in desperate need of more battery life or you use your phone a TON for videography. Otherwise keep your S22 Ultra, S21 Ultra, and Note 20 Ultra (unless you are really really finicky about having the best photo quality possible, even if only a small imprvement, and willing to pay big for it.)

Probably the most hyped improvement on this phone is having a 200 megapixel camera (this reminds me of the 'megapixel war' days of digital cameas where more didn't always mean better.) I compared photos with my 3 model generations older Note 20 Ultra with the 108mp camera and 5X zoom. You have to understand that a lot of how your image turns out can depend on if you know in what rare cases you should override using the auto settings and change the settings or use a different camera app like the Expert Raw app from the Samsung Galaxy Store. For outside photos using the main camera, the Expert Raw app set at 50 megapixel is the best quality on the S23U. For all other situations, it's safest to just use the standard camera up in auto mode except in extremely low light, go ahead and manually put the camera in night mode (it puts it automatically in that mode but it's not the same mode as manual night mode.) My Note 20 Ultra photos under close inspection actually took nearly identical quality photos as the S23 Ultra except when using the 10X zoom camera and zooming out to 15-30X. All other situations the improvement on the S23 is modest at best and virtually unnoticeable to a casual observer not comparing side by side really hard.

Also a note about "shutter lag" which seems to be the only consistent complaint about this phone (and it's predecessor.) It's really processing lag, not shutter lag and it's easily mitigated by installed the Good Lock app from the Galaxy Store app and then from Good Lock install the Camara Assistant app and change two settings: Quick Tap Shutter ON and Capture speed, change from Prioritize quality to either Balance speed and quality or priorize speed.

The video stabilization is signficantly improved also over even the S22 Ultra. So if you like to share movie clips, unedited, this is a benefit. Otherwise most any video editor and add additional stabilization.

The second most hyped feature you'll probably read about is the new CPU and its high benchmarks (along with the countless comparisons to the latest iPhone.) In reality, a phone with a CPU from 3 years ago (unless you are a gamer) is plenty fast and these are just numbers that the Samsung Marketing department or their commission earning reviewers love to tout. As far as real-world benefit there are none EXCEPT for the improvement in battery life. But that's due to EFFICIENCY not MAX PERFORMANCE.

So in a nutshell, in my opinion, if you have a 1-3 year old model, the main reasons to upgrade to this phone is if you want the longest battery life possible, or if you shoot a lot of video.

The downside to this phone is with all those cameras and the big 5000 mah battery it is a "brick" of a phone. You will get use to the weight and size after several days, but at first, even coming from an even larger screen (0.1" larger) Note 20 Ultra, the phone was noticeably thicker and heavier. This is not a great phone to be putting in your shorts pocket when you go on a run. But there's a trade off to getting the latest flagship features and seemingly endless battery life.

review_title: ITS A LENOVO PHONE! + 6 MONTHS UPDATE
review_text:
What a disappointment! My first Motorola phone in years have let me down.

Let's talk about the pros:

1) Decent small bezel screen with good resolution, 18:9 ratio is chic!

2) Almost stock Android experience, if vanilla is your favorite flavor.

5) A turbo charger is included, you can charge your phone in under an hour from 0 to 100 easily. But I think I know why it has one bundled with it...Keep reading...

Moving on to the cons, oh boy it's a long one:

1) This is the LOW-SPEC version, other market gets 4gb of ram and 64gb of storage, as well as actual glass back. This one gets 3gb/32gb and a plastic build. Yuck!

2) This phone will only get one more major Android release, the current 8.0 operating system is soooooooooooo damn slow on this phone. Like it becomes sluggish once you have a few apps open. It reminds me of using earlier Android phones. Ah, the nostalgia!

3) Camera sucks despite being a "now in season" dual cam setup. And here are MULTIPLE REASONS WHY IT SUCKS.

A, The Moto camera app takes forever to take a picture.

B, It doesn't have OIS, so all your pictures WILL be blurry. You better be steady like you have three legs (like a tripod).

C, The stock Google photo app takes FOREVER to open the picture you've just taken. Vanilla is not always good!

D, The pictures taken by default tend to be oversaturated, everyone look like they have an orange tan. As my friend puts it, the way this camera renders color is like a flip phone from the early 2000s. UNACCEPTABLE!

I usually unplug my phone at 7AM, and by 2PM I find myself having to reach for the charger. Charging the phone slowly using a standard USB charger does make the battery last a smidge longer. However, I now know why it came with a turbo charger, because you'll be needing to charge this phone quite frequently!

In conclusion,
DON'T BUY THIS PHONE if you have other choices, a similarly priced Huawei or Nokia will perform better than this fraud of a Motorola (Hint: It's actually made by lenovo, which sucks at making phones if you don't already know).

review_title: Great value for the money...A feature rich smartphone.
review_text:
My daughter is going to college after this summer. She is using a 4-year old Huawei Mate2 phone. She complains the phone's slow response. So, I am searching for a replacement phone for a while. Got this Honor View 10 on Amazon prime day event. Based on the features and capabilities this phone is offering, the $399 price is a steal.

I am not the type of person spending top dollar pursuing the latest and best models on everything, period. I am very value oriented. Like the old saying, price is what you pay, value is what you get. This phone fit's my value-seeking profile...I end up purchasing one for my daughter and....one for myself.

This Honor View 10 phone is fast. HiSilicon's Kirin 970 process is at the same class against Qualcom's Snagdragon 830 (not 845). Or better than Qualcom's older 7xx or 6xx chips still used in quite some new released phone models these days. The generous 6GB ram is definitely a key factor helping the phone run faster. Even the up-coming new iPhone (due 9/2018) comes with only 4GB ram (per industry pro's speculations). In general, big ram makes a phone more future proof as new apps tends to take more ram space.

The included 128GB storage space is not a big deal to me, but it is important for college kids as they tend to take photos, video clips a lot. Not to mention that they download tons of music, or even movies.

Yes, it has a micro SD card slot. But with 128GB space, not sure I would care about the support of micro SD card or not. Not to mention that files can be automatically backup to the cloud (the phone provides that setting.).

Yes, it comes with some pre-installed apps and some of them can't be uninstalled. But with this generous 128GB space, not a big deal to leave them there.

The capacitive-based finger print sensing/authentication technology is pretty mature at this point. This phone's finger print authenticating operation is very fast. Virtually don't feel any lag. The moment I touch the home button, the phone is unlocked.

Surprisingly, the phone comes with a facial recognition feature also. I can't comment on the false authentication rate. I perform my own limited testings, it seems working great. The facial recognition process is also very fast. Just press the power button (not the home button) and the phone is unlocked right away (as it sees me). This feature is a up-side surprise to me.

It has NFC, not sure I would use that feature for paying in supermarket using phone directly.

Battery life is good. One charge lasts for 2 days in my use case as I don't play game or watching video on smartphone.

Some people don't like the default UI, but it takes only few second to change it to generic Android UI. Not a big deal really.

Audio speaker is pretty loud. No complaint here.

During my one month ownership of this phone, Huawei has already push out one security update to my phone. That's good. I never got any system update in my previous phone (4-year ownership).

My previous phone has a 6.2 inch screen size. That is too big to carry around in my pocket. Honor View 10's 5.99 inch screen size with 16:9 screen ratio is far more easier to fit into my pocket.

I know this phone is not water-proof before I purchase. So, not really a down-side for me.

The only one feature that I hope to have is OIS (optical image stabilization). This phone does not have OIS in its camera module. However, lately (8/2018), I read news release that Huawei is releasing SW update to enable the EIS (Electrical image stabilization) function in Honor View 10. They are releasing the SW update to India market at this point to confirm the releasing process is smooth. Once that's confirmed, they will release the SW update to other markets. I look forward to using the EIS function for improving photo taking quality. Also, when taking video while walking, the video would be far more stable.

Too bad, Honor View10 does not support radio (I know this before purchasing). No kidding here, I listen to radio using my previous smart phone. I am using a small portable radio device now.

All in all, with $399 price, this phone is really a great value buy. With the up-coming EIS feature included, I really don't have any complaint for this phone.

*****

Just found out the latest system update (Build# C567) already released the EIS feature. Open the camera app, tap video selection, open the setting. Scroll down the settings, there is a "Stabilizer" option. The EIS is available for video with 1080p at 30pf.

Does it "work"? Sure. You can call on it, send and receive emails, take photos, surf the web, download apps. Yes, it works. It's a little like comparing an Atari videogame from the 1980s to the current state of the art, or using a computer running an ancient operating system.

I understand that not everyone needs, or can afford, a top of the line smartphone. However, the additional cost of a phone that's substantially easier to use--larger screen, faster, more up to date software--really isn't that much. This is a product review, but first I wanna discuss my satisfaction with the fact that this is a renewed item.

Overall, I'm happy buying this renewed, saved myself 50% of the brand new price.

As for reviewing the phone itself, this is my first Samsung phone, I've never so much as seen a Galaxy Note with my own eyes, and therefore I'm still learning things about it. Since the fingerprint scanner is located inside the screen, you can't just get a traditional otterbox case for this phone, the heavy duty screen protector doesn't allow fingerprint scanning, so you have to buy a specific stick-on screen protector. I like having all the extra storage on the phone, in the past I always felt like my phone filled up with stuff too quickly. This phone came pre-loaded with a few useless apps, but didn't come pre-loaded with all the other useful apps that generally come on androids like a music player, Amazon, and other such...loaded it myself. I ended up loading Samsung Music...which I already love way more than iTunes or Apple Music.

I'm still learning how to use the stylus pen, believe me, there is a TON of ways to use the pen, but from what I've tried so far, it's great! review_title: Sexy and useless, bad for your eyes
review_text:
This sexy, classy device hides a multitude of shortcomings.
Pure is a Windows device and as such promises to provide a useful PDA replacement. The Windows Mobile operating system permits storage, organization and even editing of documents, which can be transferred by cable or blue tooth. The phone comes with a desktop sync application, which I did not get around to trying, but probably works adequately.
There are quite a few negatives.
First: Size. The screen is so small that editing or reading your applications requires magnification. It is less useful than it sounds.
Software/Operating system: I had to replace the first unit I purchased, as the system caused unwelcome programs to open in the middle of other processes. Having experienced this on a Trio, I wouldn't take the chance of this recurring out of warranty.
Resolution: I spent a jet lagged hour playing the game included in the software. I noticed that I was having problems seeing the screen, but it was not until I put it down that I realized that I was seeing everything double and blurred, a condition which lasted a few hours. A subsequent trip to the eye clinic put my mind at rest regarding my eyes. Prescription: "Get a different phone".
Battery life: I have had any number of phones, smart and dumb, and any number of PDA's (which I had hoped to replace with this). None have run out of power so quickly.
Unlocking: I travel on business, hence the need for a phone with PDA features. Like all international travelers, I carry overseas sim cards with minutes for my stays. This phone at the time I purchased it was extremely difficult to unlock. As a matter of fact, it took the techie several days to get the code, which did not to get to me. I was out $40 with a locked phone. This was fortunate, as it permitted me to return it.
The AT&T plan. AT&T's recent announcement that all users of Smart Phones, even if they decided they did not want the Internet services, would have to pay the extra $30, which after tax and fees is $40 per month for the Data Plan. This phone could have WiFi, but at $480/year AT&T is motivated not to offer the most customer friendly option.
Keyboard: Even with slender fingers, I hit it wrong plenty of times. Very annoying.
Memory.The phone has essentially no memory, which is odd for a Windows machine, but this goes with the size. A memory card will set you back anywhere upwards of $40 for anything useful.
Price: This phone is valued at $500, although AT&T is currently giving it away for $.01 on Amazon in the cutthroat race for customers. This with a two year plan. If you really want a useful item and are willing to sell your soul to T for twenty four months, consider as an alternative Blackberry. (The extra $40 /month applies.)

My solution: I decided to continue as I had been, with phone and PDA separate. I am forcing IPod Touch into the role of PDA (DocumentsToGo, HandBase for the database functions, Easy Reader and other relatively cheap apps make this possible). IPod Touch has bluetooth, WiFi, 16gb memory.

review_title: Poor voice and LTE signal reception
review_text:
I bought this device direct from Motorola. This is the 3rd phone I've owned in the Motorola G family. The first was the original G7, the second the 2019 version of the Motorola G Power and the third... was this one, the Moto G Power (2021 edition). I expected incremental improvements but I was fundamentally wrong.

The camera continues to suck and its AI is laughable - especially at night. Compared alongside an iPhone XS Max the difference is day-and-night (especially night) with the iPhone taking so much better photos that I eventually dug out my old iPhone 7 to create some context. The iPhone 7 was significantly superior except in terms of native resolution. In particular the iPhones are better at scene composition/lighting and target focusing.

However this wasn't the worst problem. I found the radio reception (voice and LTE) was very marginal and inferior to ALL other Motorola G series phones I've owned to-date. In marginal areas, where the G7 produced crystal clear voice and decent LTE speeds (comparable to the iPhone XS Max) the Moto G Power (2021) was unable to make a voice connect and there was 'no internet' reported (aka no LTE).

So ONE MONTH after I bought the Moto G Power (2021) I wanted rid of it. I thought maybe I could trade-in with Motorola, but no, the phone isn't on their list of applicable trade-ins. I can guess why! So I'm very disappointed with Motorola. I was hoping to trade up to the Motorola One 5g ace, but with no trade-in path for a brand new phone I wasn't going to cough up full price replacing what is essentially a product dud.

I should say that in strong signal areas the Moto G Power (2021) worked fine, both voice and data, so I have to suspect that Motorola made design compromises to extend battery life (which, btw, is superb).

Finally I should add that most of the Motorola phones (at the lower and mid levels) come with Android 10 which is already out-of-date. I suspect this has something to do with memory. The Moto G Power (2021) comes with 4G of RAM but perhaps Android 11 prefers more? Honestly don't know.

So overall this phone has only two strong points. The amazing battery life and the relatively speedy processor (considering it's a low end product). But these can't compensate for a fundamental deficit in radio/data communications. If you want a long battery life I'd recommend you get the 2019 version of this phone which works fine for radio/data and has almost no drawbacks compared to the 2021 version.

The Sony Xperia 1 is a stunning smartphone. It comes in a beautiful, near bezel-less frame with a 6.5 inch screen and a unique 21:9 aspect ratio. It features a 4K OLED screen and quality speakers for an optimal movie-watching experience. However, it lacks a 3.5mm audio jack, so you will need either Bluetooth headphones or a headphone jack to USB-C dongle. It comes pre-loaded with Android Pie (v9.0) out of the box. The Xperia 1 has 6 gigabytes of RAM and 128 gigabytes of internal storage, which can be expanded with a micro-SD card. It also features a 12 megapixel camera with three lenses for zoom and low-level light situations. The 6GB RAM makes the Xperia 1 great for gaming; I have yet to experience any lag or slowdown while playing, and the phone rarely heats up while in use. The camera is specially designed for recording video, and comes with an onboard video editor. Streaming movies is great with the 21:9 aspect ratio, but when streaming YouTube or other videos, you will experience some letterboxing while watching. Videos shot in the usual 16:9 ratio will leave black bars on either end of your screen. It's tolerable, but watching videos in the 4:3 ratio will leave nearly half of the screen unused. Although the Xperia 1 is tall, it still feels great to hold, even with one hand. There are several tap and swipe gestures implemented to make operating the phone easier with one hand. The battery life is about average. You can expect about 4-5 hours of straight, screen-on use, or a day's worth of normal usage. The USB-C connector allows for quick charging. You can get a full charge in less than 2 hours. The only nitpicks I have with the phone is that the screen does not get very bright, and that the phone automatically restarts every time the SIM card is inserted or removed. Overall, I really like the Sony Xperia 1 and would recommend it to others. It may not be for everyone, but it's a solid smartphone that is great for watching movies.

review_title: UMIDIGI F1 Play, camera up to 48 MP in a mid-range mobile
review_text:
UMIDIGI F1 Play is a “Premium” mid-range phone that stands out for combining powerful hardware with 6 GB of RAM and 64 GB of storage, while its 5150 mAh battery with support for fast charging ensures great autonomy and Its double rear camera with 48 megapixel sensor is up to the highest demands of users.

Notch design and reduced bezels

The aesthetics of this terminal adapts to current market trends from a reduction of its bezels along its four faces and a water drop shaped notch on the upper margin to integrate its front camera.

UMIDIGI F1 Play is sold in two colors, red and black, while its official dimensions respond to 15.70 x 7.50 x 0.90 cm with a total weight of 187 grams.

Being part of both its aesthetics and its performance, it is necessary to focus on the screen present in this device when it occupies 92.7% of the total frontal surface. The IPS panel is 6.3 inches in size with a Full HD + resolution and an extended aspect ratio of 19.5: 9 for better viewing.

Performance boosted

UMIDIGI F1 Play once again makes use of a processor signed by MediaTek, more precisely the P60 model that has been manufactured in a 12-nanometer architecture and consists of eight cores at a frequency of 2.0 GHz. In relation to the previous generation ensures lower energy consumption and less heating to demanding tasks.

On the other hand, it is complemented by 6 GB of RAM, a clear improvement over the standard UMIDIGI F1, GPU Mali G72 MP3 and a total of 64 GB of internal storage that should be more than enough for the average user to host a great variety of applications and multimedia content inside.

The battery is one of the protagonists of this Smartphone by adding a capacity of 5,150 mAh, that is to say autonomy for several days with an average use. As if that were not enough, its fast charging capacity at 18W avoids long periods of waiting time to reuse the mobile.

Cameras and more extra details

Turning to its camera configuration, another of the great novelties in this UMIDIGI F1 Play is the evolution of its dual rear sensor to include a main 48 megapixel. Excellent results are promised even in conditions with very little lighting, while its long aperture f / 1.7 allows nothing to remain out of focus. Meanwhile, the second sensor is 8 megapixels.

If what interests you are the selfies, professional-type captures are also possible thanks to a 16 megapixel sensor with f / 2.0 aperture and inclusion of an algorithm that is responsible for improving real-time shots with greater clarity and natural effects.

It should be noted that in addition to the fingerprint sensor present on the center of its back face, there is also support for facial recognition technology that automatically analyzes the parameters of the user's face to offer a complementary method of security and privacy.

Finally, the Smartphone arrives with Android 9.0 Pie factory installed to access the latest developments at the level of Google OS software, while the NFC connection not only guarantees pairing between devices in one touch but also the possibility of performing mobile payments through the Google Play platform.

PROS:

Dual rear camera with 48 MP sensor

Large capacity battery

Fluid performance thanks to its 6 GB of RAM

Competitive price

CONS:

Your processor could be something more powerful

There are times when the cell phone camera does not perform as well as I would like it to perform, however the majority of the time the camera does an excellent job. I like all the overall features of the phone in general, but the camera is especially important to me.
Original review:
I am still getting familiar with this cellphone. I am using AT&T cellphone service. I had to ask for help from a sales rep in the AT&T store because the SIM card is a different size as compared with the one in my Galaxy S5 Active. This review is not meant to be comprehensive, but I hope to touch on a few key points. First off, the camera. There are a lot of hidden features including a professional setting that allows the user to change from auto to macro or infinity or somewhere in between, adjust the ISO, the white balance or the brightness. I have personally not seen these features to be of much value yet. Sure you can use the white balance, but then you might lose some of the sharpness in your photo (in the sky, for instance). There is a slow motion setting and panorama option as well. After you take a photo, you can select different editing features such as cropping, different coloration, black and white or sketch mode. I have not tried the slow motion, professional or panorama features yet. These photos
were taken with auto setting in 16:9 with 9 megapixels. I tested the video feature and it worked fine. I am missing a few features of my Samsung Galaxy S5, especially the voice command option for taking a photo. This phone is set up with Google Voice, so you can say "Ok, Google, take a picture" and the camera will open up, but you still need to tap the screen or tap the shutter button. You set up for either tapping anywhere on the screen or using the shutter button. The burst mode allows you to take multiple photos at lightning speed. The camera is super fast. What I don't like as compared with my S5 is that you really can't
focus in well on one object in the picture, but with some practice, I may figure this out. I added a salt grinder photo taken with macro setting. Update: I tried the panorama and professional settings as well as the 8x zoom. The panorama option is very easy and works well as long as you can keep a straight line of view. The zoom lens can make the camera a bit shaky, so it might be good to compare using the zoom vs cropping a photo afterwards. I wish that the camera offered grid lines as a guide for keeping the horizon straight. Unfortunately I have not been able to upload new photos to my review. I have been really pleased with some landscape and close ups in outdoor lighting. The images are easily enhanced with editing features. Many of my up
close flower photos have been relatively sharp. I like Google Voice and use it often for asking about the weather, searching for a song, or finding a business phone number, for example. Addressing the 4GB of RAM - the settings show the average amount of RAM used. I am using 2 GB of RAM on average, therefore I would have been using 100% of RAM with my old phone. With the 64 GB of internal memory, I can now install the apps that will want and not receive constant warnings that I am running out of storage space. So far the phone is fast and responsive for wifi and data. Update: July 18, 2017: I am still trying to work with all the features of this phone. I still like using my Samsung Galaxy S5 for photos in addition to this cellphone. Both phones have
their pluses and minuses for camera features. The Moto G5 screen is shiny and has a lot of glare and it's dark, so it's very hard to view in bright sunlight. When taking photos, I am often merely pointing and shooting and hoping for a good outcome. Maybe there is a setting change that will adjust for this. The photos came out fine, but using the 16x9 9-megapixel feature, cropping and zooming can result in very blurry photos. Also the selfie front camera takes clear photos, but there is distortion due to a wide angle lens, so you end up with a fun snapshot, not a great photo by any means. The nice thing about the selfie feature is that the camera blurs all skin imperfections - like a beauty mode. That said, that the faces end up looking a little distorted - but, hey - at least you can get a few people in a photo easily!
I opted for the pattern security (connect the dots with finger swipe) rather than the thumb print, but may reevaluate this. Update: I have set up security for in home use with no pattern required as well as facial recognition. We will see how it goes. I was constantly having to swipe the pattern to access my phone.
One negative so far is that the head phone jack seems a little stubborn with certain mp3 cords or headphones. I had to play around a bit with the mp3 cord in my car to get it to work. Then I had to turn the volume up quite a bit.
As others have commented, the speaker is not very loud. That said, the phone seems to have clear sound for listening to the phone receiver - just not overly loud. I tested the speaker and my 84 year old father could hear me just fine and I could hear him. That was indoors with the TV at low volume.
Update:
I tested out the video and taking photos of fireworks and golf swings. The video in outdoor lighting appeared somewhat dark and I am not sure how to compensate for this. Fireworks looked more like explosions in the sky - fuzzy and none of the crispness of a newer IPhone. On the other hand, the phone worked well for capturing the last part of a golf swing and I could have utilized the burst feature easily but forgot. The result was a true action shot.
Editing photos also serves to enhance the quality, but on occasion making changes seems to take forever. My phone ended in a loop and I had to turn it off and restart. Dusk photos of people and the sky were also somewhat grainy. The flash is fairly bright for up close photos, though. The front facing camera for selfies works really well in outdoor lighting - haven't tried indoors yet.
Update - Nov 29, 2017: I have now been using this phone on a very regular basis since I purchased it in July of 2017. It has proven to be very reliable. As I stated previously, the zoom feature does not appear to be of any great value and also the video quality is not good at all in a dark setting such as viewing a concert in a theater. I am comparing this phone with my Samsung Galaxy S5 that actually shines in dark settings even with zooming in on a band performing. For this reason I end up taking my old phone with me if I want to do any video. Maybe there is some setting that I am missing. Other than that, the phone is consistently good for everyday use. I'm constantly getting praise for my photos which I can easily edit with the Google editing features.

Switched that to off and the sound on notification messaging works now, while wearing my watch. Hope this is a long time fix. Phone has nice upgrades, including Face ID, fingerprint reader on the side now and better battery life. Getting use to no more home button but it's an upgrade.

review_text:
This phone replaces an Alcatel PIXI that I upgraded to a month ago. For $15 you definitely get what you pay for. I was surprised that a smartphone could be acquired for so little money. That phone was slow reacting and just didn't have enough memory to truly be functional even after adding a 32 GB Micro SD card. That is probably why it was so cheap. At lease I wasn't out much money other the extra batteries I purchased for it.
I am very happy with Galaxy J3 Luna Pro. With the larger memory I was able to load all the apps and data that I am used to having on my "mind that remembers." I moved every app that was available to be moved to the SD card. It now has 4.9 GB available on the internal memory and 26.2 GB available on the SD card. I really don't know why the manufacturers advertised phones with 16 GB internal memory when 60% of that space is taken up by the OS and bloatware. That means a 16 GB phone actually has 6.4 GB available for your apps and data. No wonder the Alcatel was under performing with its 8 GB.
One reason I bought this phone is that it was it came 1000 minutes, 2000 texts and 2 GB of Data. I thought I had the Wi-Fi off when I started loading apps. I blew away over 1 GB of data setting it up. DAMN ! Make sure you turn off Mobile Data for all you data miser’s out there.
I like that the phone has a replaceable battery and a SD car slot. Something that my S6 did not have. After a year of use, the S6’s run time dropped to where I had to charge it daily and sometimes the same day when it was under heavy use. Pros: Features rare for a phone at this price range-- fingerprint scanner, 1080p screen, 4 gb memory, and a 3000 mAh battery. Has a look and feel similar to some older iPhone models.

Cons: The 430 processor is on the low end compared to the 600 & 800 series out now, and it struggles with media heavy web-pages. Camera is below average-- a fine example of why megapixels counts are often meaningless. Display blurs slightly with fast moving content. Questionable quality (see below).

Update: The phone stopped booting about six months after buying it. The issue resembled a corrupt OS, but factory wiping it had no effect. Blu customer support said it was likely a hardware problem, and offered to fix it under warranty. However, since they said the turn-around time would be several weeks, I recycled the phone instead. A good phone while it lasted.
